newsitem.title: USA: Economic impact of new GM strike seen slight.
newsitem.headline: Economic impact of new GM strike seen slight.

text.p: The impact on the United States economy of a fresh strike against General Motors Corp by workers at a giant sport/utility vehicle plant in Moraine, Ohio is likely to be slighter than the effect from the strike by Canadian autoworkers against the automaker in the fall of 1996, economists and analysts said on Monday.

The strike by nearly 4,100 people, begun on Sunday and ordered by the International Union of Electronics Workers after workers voted not to ratify a new labor pact, is at a final assembly plant, not one that produces parts needed by other GM factories.
Thus, in contrast to the October 1996 strike, other auto plants will not have to shut down because of a lack of parts for their own operations, analysts said.

"The effects of this strike don't radiate out to GM broadly," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc. "It doesn't threaten to shut down GM -- which the strike against the parts plants did.
"On the other hand," said Lieberman, "this plant does assemble sport/utility vehicles which happen to be the strongest part of the motor vehicle market."
"The strike matters to GM because their profits are built on sport/utility vehicles," agreed Peter D'Antonio, senior economist at Citicorp Global Finance N.A.
But how, or even whether, the strike affects broad economic statistics on the U.S. economy, depends on how long it lasts, economists said.

"It's definitely too soon to tell," said Lieberman. "Clearly it has the potential to be disruptive. But if work stops for just a day or two, it's a very different situation from what happens if it lasts a week or more."
The strike by Canadian workers against General Motors depressed auto industrial production numbers in the U.S. for October. But output bounced back once the strike was settled.
"In October, the strike definitely curbed industrial production," said Lieberman. "But, of course, once the strike settled, industrial production rebounded."
"When all was said and done, the October strike didn't make a lot of statistical impact," said Raymond Worseck, chief economist at St. Louis, Mo.-based A.G. Edwards & Sons.
Even GM does not depend on the Ohio plant for all its sports/utility vehicle production.
The popular Chevrolet Blazer and GMC Jimmy compact sport/utility models are also produced at a New Jersey GM plant represented by the United Auto Workers union.
For the strike to really matter, it would have to be at a plant that manufactures parts, said D'Antonio.
"The (parts) suppliers hold more power," he said.

Four thousand workers also would not sway U.S. monthly payroll data, said D'Antonio. And since strikers cannot collect unemployment insurance in Ohio, the work stoppage also will not affect weekly claims for jobless benefits.
